description: baseline (scaffold RandomForest, 3 features)
hypothesis: the scaffold reproduces the sibling trees' accuracy exactly (same split, same model) and fails physics, because a tree is piecewise constant and saturates outside the 0.5 mi training range while the sweep runs to 5 mi
observation: rmse 0.013345 / trip_rmse 0.003037, identical to both sibling trees; 6 of 9 checks fail, led by climb_floor at 81.1% and round_trip_convexity at 45.7%, with implied eta_drive 1.290 and length_invariance 8.83
reasoning: the dominant failure is not extrapolation but the grade response itself: an implied drivetrain efficiency of 1.29 means the forest bills a climb for less than the height it gains at every distance, so no amount of range extension fixes it - the functional form has to encode gravity

description: structured physics parametrization: 4 bounded heads (A,B,C,T) driven by an MLP
hypothesis: predicting E = d*(A + B*g+ - C*g-) + T with each head squashed into its physically legal interval satisfies all nine checks by construction, because the ceiling in physics.py decomposes into exactly the same d-proportional and d-fixed parts
observation: physics_pass 1.0 with every violation rate at 0.0 and length_invariance exactly 0.0, at rmse 0.013397 (+0.39%) and trip_rmse 0.003060 (+0.76%) against the unconstrained forest; 389s of the 600s budget
reasoning: the guarantee held algebraically on the first try, and the accuracy cost of being physically legal is under 1% even with the network seeing only speed - grade and length are carried entirely by the structure, so all the remaining capacity is free for information the baseline never had

description: add prev_speed_mph to the network inputs
hypothesis: acceleration is the dominant unmeasured driver of link energy (both sibling trees), and the T head is exactly the per-link transient energy, so the entry speed should feed it directly without needing a per-mile kinetic term
observation: rmse -19.3% and trip_rmse -1.7%, physics still passing on every check; length_invariance moved 0.0 -> 3.31 because T became non-zero
reasoning: the split is the classic information signature - a large rmse gain with almost none at trip level - and the length_invariance move is the structure working as intended, since a non-zero fixed cost T makes the per-mile rate genuinely higher on short links

description: add next_speed_mph (the exit half of the kinetic delta)
hypothesis: this tree has no one-link-lookback restriction, so the exit speed is available; the unguided tree's best single feature was two-sided, so the exit half should still carry signal after the entry half is in
observation: rmse -4.7% and trip_rmse -4.6%, moving together for the first time this session; physics still clean
reasoning: the exit-side gain is about a quarter of the entry-side gain, matching the sibling trees' 2-4x entry-over-exit ratio, and the fact that trip_rmse moved as far as rmse suggests the exit speed removes a *systematic* bias - links that end in braking were previously overbilled everywhere

description: add prev_miles (reliability context for prev_speed_mph)
hypothesis: prev_miles tells the model how much to trust prev_speed_mph as an estimate of the speed at the previous link's end, and was a top-3 feature in both sibling trees
observation: rmse -3.1% but trip_rmse +0.31%, so not Pareto-dominant; length_invariance collapsed 2.63 -> 0.59, meaning the model moved a lot of its explanation out of the fixed T term and into the per-mile rate A
reasoning: the length_invariance collapse is the tell: prev_miles lets the model resolve per-link error by re-attributing energy from T to A, which sharpens individual links but shifts a small systematic bias into every link of a trip at once - exactly the error mode trip_rmse is sensitive to; worth re-testing once something else has moved trip_rmse

description: add prev2_speed_mph (the approach profile)
hypothesis: the speed two links back describes how the vehicle approached, and was worth -4.6% in the unguided tree
observation: rmse -0.42% and trip_rmse +0.07%, so a near-tie that is not Pareto-dominant
reasoning: worth ten times less here than in the unguided tree, and the reason is structural: there the second-order approach information had to be inferred from raw speeds, while here T is already an explicit per-link transient energy that prev_speed and next_speed pin down directly - the second-order term has almost nothing left to add

description: let the climb term spend the flat rate's unused ceiling headroom
hypothesis: pinning the climb slope to [k_pot, k_pot/eta_peak] says a climb never costs more than mgh at peak drivetrain efficiency, but a real climb runs the motor off its peak; if that bound binds it is a signed bias on every graded link, which is exactly what trip_rmse punishes
observation: both metrics improved but only by ~0.15%; implied_eta_drive moved from 1.000 (pinned at the old bound) to 0.895, so the extra headroom is genuinely being spent
reasoning: keep, but the small size is the more useful result: the climb slope was barely binding, so the remaining trip_rmse error is not in the grade response - the diagnostic value of this experiment exceeded its accuracy value

description: signed transient: let a link give back the kinetic energy it releases
hypothesis: with T >= 0 and A >= res/2, a flat link could never be predicted below half its road load, yet a quarter of the data is at or below zero - the model was structurally unable to express regen, and gating a negative T on the kinetic energy actually released (zero at steady state, so zero on the sweep) unlocks it without touching the guarantee
observation: rmse -26.2% and trip_rmse -14.9%, the largest move of the session, with every physics check still passing
reasoning: this was a missing *sign*, not missing information - the same three speeds were already inputs, and all that changed is that the structure now lets their difference come out negative; the lesson is to audit a constrained parametrization for what it cannot represent before adding features to it

description: re-test prev_miles under the signed-transient structure
hypothesis: prev_miles was discarded at exp4 for a 0.31% trip_rmse regression, and the sibling trees' rule is that a marginal feature is tuned against an architecture rather than against the problem; the signed transient changed the architecture materially, so it should be re-measured
observation: rmse -8.8% and trip_rmse -5.1%, where the same feature previously bought -3.1% rmse at the cost of trip_rmse
reasoning: prev_miles says how much to trust prev_speed as the speed at the previous link's end, and that only pays once the model has something quantitative to do with the entry speed - before exp7 it could only add energy, so a sharper entry estimate had nowhere useful to go

description: add next_miles (the exit-side reliability context)
hypothesis: next_miles is to next_speed_mph what prev_miles is to prev_speed_mph - how far the neighbour ran is how much to trust its average as the speed at the shared boundary - and the exit side matters more here than in the sibling trees because the released-kinetic term reads next_speed directly
observation: rmse -2.5% and trip_rmse -1.2%, about a third of what prev_miles was worth
reasoning: the entry-over-exit ratio is holding at roughly 3x across every paired feature this session (speed, miles), which matches the sibling trees and the physics: acceleration into a link is billed to it in full, while braking out of it is split with the next link by regen

description: size the kinetic release from the link's own peak, not just its entry
hypothesis: a link that accelerates above both neighbours and then brakes releases kinetic energy that max(ke(prev) - ke(next), 0) scores as zero, so widening the gate to the link's own average speed should let those links be predicted lower
observation: rmse tied to six decimals and trip_rmse -0.44%, so a weak Pareto win; run time also fell to 178s, which is machine load rather than the model
reasoning: kept because it is one extra maximum() for a real trip-level gain, but the size says most released energy is already visible in the entry-to-exit difference - the accelerate-then-brake link is a minority case, and it moves trip_rmse rather than rmse because it corrects a small bias spread over many links

description: re-test prev2_speed_mph under the signed-transient structure
hypothesis: prev2_speed_mph tied at exp5 under the old structure; the same re-test rule that made prev_miles pay at exp8 should apply, since the model can now do something signed with an approach profile
observation: rmse -2.6% and trip_rmse -0.8%, where it was a tie before; length_invariance also fell an order of magnitude to 0.064
reasoning: second re-test to flip from tie to keep after exp7 - the signed transient did not just add accuracy, it changed which features are worth anything, and every feature screened before exp7 is now stale; the length_invariance collapse says the model is explaining more with the per-mile rate and less with the fixed cost, i.e. it is resolving *which* links really accelerate

description: add next2_speed_mph (the departure profile)
hypothesis: the exit-side analogue of prev2_speed_mph: whether braking continues past the next link says how much of this link's exit speed is really given back rather than carried on
observation: rmse -1.4% and trip_rmse -0.9%, about half of what prev2 was worth
reasoning: the entry-over-exit ratio has now held at 2-3x for three matched pairs, and the +/-2 window is still paying about half of what +/-1 did, so the chain has not been exhausted at two links out

description: add prev_grade_percent (the terrain behind the vehicle)
hypothesis: the current link's grade is structural and cannot enter the heads, but the previous link's grade can, and it says whether the vehicle arrived carrying momentum off a descent - information the neighbour speeds average away
observation: rmse -0.15% but trip_rmse -0.89%, six times the link-level gain; the unguided tree measured prev_grade at roughly zero
reasoning: the lopsided split is the signature of removing systematic bias rather than adding information: terrain is spatially correlated, so a whole trip through hills was being biased the same direction on every link, and correcting that shows up at trip level - which is also why the unguided tree, scoring an unstructured rate, could not find it

description: add next_grade_percent (the terrain ahead)
hypothesis: the exit-side analogue of prev_grade_percent, which was worth -0.89% trip_rmse one experiment earlier
observation: an exact tie on trip_rmse and 0.03% worse on rmse - the first paired feature this session where the exit side was worth nothing at all rather than a third of the entry side
reasoning: grade breaks the entry/exit symmetry that speed and length both follow, and the asymmetry is causal: the terrain behind determines the momentum the vehicle actually arrives with, while the terrain ahead only matters through the exit speed, which next_speed_mph and next2_speed_mph already state directly

description: widen the network 128 -> 256
hypothesis: nine network inputs against 128 hidden units, and the sibling tree found 256 optimal at eleven features, so the model may be capacity-limited
observation: rmse +0.8% and trip_rmse -0.6%, the exact split the unguided tree reported for every capacity increase it tried; length_invariance jumped an order of magnitude to 1.22
reasoning: capacity past its optimum chases per-link noise, which the equally-weighted rmse punishes and the mileage-weighted trip_rmse averages away; the length_invariance jump is the mechanism made visible - the wider net spent its extra capacity making the fixed cost T vary more sharply, which is exactly per-link noise-fitting

description: halve the epoch budget 300 -> 150
hypothesis: run for half the epochs to find out whether the fit is converged, and if it is, spend the freed budget on a second ensemble member - ensembling is free in this tree because inference cost is not an objective here
observation: both metrics regressed (rmse +0.5%, trip_rmse +1.3%), so 300 epochs is not slack; separately the run took 98s where identical code took 429s at exp12, a 2.4x swing in machine load
reasoning: the ensemble plan dies on the load variance rather than on the metrics - two 300-epoch members would fit comfortably at the fast end and truncate against TRAIN_SECONDS_CAP at the slow end, making the result depend on who else is using the GPU; a single model is the only reproducible option, and the epoch count stays where it is

description: add entry_kinetic_gge (signed kinetic work of entering the link)
hypothesis: the sibling rule is to hand-engineer only what the network cannot cheaply approximate; the structure already divides a fixed energy by distance, but squaring a speed is not free, so the difference of squares should be given directly
observation: rmse -0.19% and trip_rmse -0.14%, a weak Pareto win
reasoning: kept but marginal - far smaller than the same feature was worth in the sibling trees, because there it also carried the division by distance that made it hard; here the structure already performs that division, so all that is left is the squaring, and a 128-unit ReLU net approximates a square well enough that handing it over is worth almost nothing

description: add sinuosity (path length over straight-line endpoint distance)
hypothesis: the domain-guided tree got -1.3% on both metrics from sinuosity, and a winding link makes the vehicle corner, which is speed variation the link average hides - exactly what the transient heads are for
observation: rmse -1.9% and trip_rmse -2.2%, larger than in the sibling tree and the biggest feature gain since exp9
reasoning: worth more here than there because the structure gives it somewhere specific to go - cornering is kinetic energy given up and recovered, which is now a signed term rather than something to be absorbed into a general-purpose rate; note the sweep has no geometry column, so predict() supplies sinuosity 1.0, which is correct because a synthetic link is straight

description: add junction_turn_degrees (the turn into the link)
hypothesis: the heading change from the previous link's exit segment into this link's entry segment was worth -4.3% rmse in the domain-guided tree, and a sharp turn is a deceleration no link average shows
observation: rmse -1.1% and trip_rmse -0.2%; the first run also revealed that decoding the geometry twice had pushed training into its time cap, so the decode was made once-per-frame and the experiment re-run - identical metrics, 47s recovered
reasoning: a quarter of what it was worth in the sibling tree, and the reason is that this model already has both neighbour speeds and both neighbour lengths, so most of what a turn implies about the speed profile is already stated; the run-time lesson is separate and worth keeping - a feature's decode cost competes with the training budget, so shared preprocessing has to be shared in fact and not just in intent

description: raise the learning rate 1e-3 -> 2e-3
hypothesis: the learning rate has never been touched and both sibling trees found it mattered; with cosine annealing to zero a larger initial step may reach a better basin within the same 300 epochs
observation: rmse +0.10% and trip_rmse -0.56% - the same trade the width increase produced at exp15, in the same direction and roughly the same ratio
reasoning: step size behaves like capacity in this model, which closes the size axis without a third run: width up and learning rate up both buy trip_rmse with rmse, so 128 units at 1e-3 is the Pareto knee and narrowing or slowing would only make the same trade in reverse; note this is the opposite of the unguided tree, where raising the tree learning rate at fixed rounds went the other way

description: a third hidden layer
hypothesis: depth is an inductive-bias change rather than a size change, so it may not reproduce the trade that width and learning rate both produced
observation: it reproduced it exactly - rmse +0.35%, trip_rmse -1.16% - and trip_rmse has now improved monotonically across all three capacity-shaped changes (0.002161 -> 0.002149 -> 0.002136) while rmse worsened each time
reasoning: three different knobs giving one signature is a mechanism, not a coincidence: extra capacity reduces regional bias, which trip_rmse rewards, while fitting per-link noise, which rmse punishes; the fix implied is variance reduction without added bias, i.e. averaging - and that can be tested at constant compute by splitting the epoch budget across two members instead of buying more capacity

description: average 2 members at half the epochs each (constant compute)
hypothesis: three capacity-shaped changes all bought trip_rmse with rmse, which says the limit is variance on one metric and bias on the other; averaging cuts variance without adding bias, and it can be paid for at constant compute by halving the epochs per member - worth noting every physics check is a linear inequality in the prediction, so an average of legal models is legal
observation: the trade reversed - rmse -0.13% and trip_rmse +0.46% - which is exactly what exp16 predicted for half-length training
reasoning: this brackets the frontier from the other side: adding capacity buys trip_rmse with rmse, and cutting convergence buys rmse with trip_rmse, so the current single 300-epoch 128-unit model sits on the knee and no reallocation of the same compute improves both; a joint win now has to come from information or structure, not from tuning

description: add prev_sinuosity (the shape of the road behind)
hypothesis: sinuosity was the best feature since exp9, and the entry side has beaten the exit side for every paired feature, so the previous link's shape should carry the same kind of signal - a winding approach means the vehicle arrives having already given up speed to corner
observation: rmse -0.51% and trip_rmse -0.37%, both real; run time 469s against a 470s training cap
reasoning: a quarter of what the link's own sinuosity was worth, which is the usual entry-side ratio, so the geometry family is behaving like the speed and length families; separately the run time is now brushing the cap and needs watching before a truncated run is mistaken for a bad idea

description: add next_junction_turn_degrees (the turn waiting at the link's end)
hypothesis: the turn recorded against the next link is the turn at the end of this one, and braking for it happens during this link and is billed to it
observation: both metrics improved (-0.53% / -0.19%) but physics_pass went to 0.0 - flat_energy_positive failed on 2.9% of cases, worst -1.3e-05 GGE on a 0.01 mi link at 20 mph, all of it at short distances
reasoning: the feature is not the culprit; it exposed a latent defect introduced at exp10. Widening the release gate to max(ke(prev), ke(v)) - ke(next) broke the invariant the whole guarantee rests on: under the 0-fill convention a synthetic sweep link has prev = next = 0, so the widened gate evaluates to ke(v) rather than zero, and the model has been free to predict negative flat-ground energy since exp10 without happening to do so. A discard under rule 1, and the defect is fixed next rather than the feature abandoned

description: narrow the release gate back to the neighbours, restoring the by-construction guarantee
hypothesis: reverting exp10's widened gate should restore released == 0 on the sweep, making flat_energy_positive true by construction again, at the cost of roughly the 0.44% trip_rmse exp10 bought
observation: rmse -0.10% and trip_rmse +0.42%, the mirror image of exp10 as expected, with physics passing; neither version dominates the other on the metrics
reasoning: kept on the tiebreak rather than on the metrics. The two are non-dominated, and the deciding fact is that exp24 showed the wider gate lets the model predict negative level-ground energy the moment the feature set changes - e007655 was passing by accident, not by construction. In a tree whose whole point is enforced physics, a guarantee that holds for any input beats 0.42% of trip_rmse that holds until the next experiment

description: re-test next_junction_turn_degrees under the restored guarantee
hypothesis: exp24's physics failure was caused by the exp10 gate, not by this feature, so with the gate narrowed the same feature should keep cleanly
observation: rmse -0.38% and trip_rmse -0.23% with physics passing - the feature was innocent, and it is worth about a third of the entry-side turn
reasoning: confirms the exp24 diagnosis rather than merely working around it; the general lesson is that a physics failure names the check, not the change, and the change that surfaces a latent defect is usually not the change that introduced it

description: give the descent the saturating shape regen_ceiling itself uses
hypothesis: regen saturates - a descent recovers road-load work at 1/eta but leftover height only at eta, so the marginal return bends once the hill outruns the road load it offsets, and a linear C*g cannot bend; capping by the climb cost at the same grade magnitude keeps round_trip_convexity
observation: rmse tied and trip_rmse +0.14%, so a discard; epochs completed 300/300, confirming the raised time cap no longer binds
reasoning: the descent side is now closed from two directions - exp6 showed the climb bound was barely binding, and this shows the descent *shape* does not matter either, both consistent with implied_eta_regen sitting at 0.82 against a 0.917 cap; grade is simply well determined by the potential-energy term and there is nothing left for the model to learn about it
